title: Gradient
wiki_lead:
In vector calculus, the gradient ∇f of a scalar-valued differentiable function f of several variables is the vector field (or vector-valued function) whose value at a point p gives the direction and the rate of fastest increase. The nabla symbol ∇, pronounced "del", denotes the vector differential operator.
If the gradient of a function is non-zero at a point p, the direction of the gradient is the direction in which the function increases most quickly from p, and the magnitude of the gradient is the rate of increase in that direction, the greatest absolute directional derivative.
This property of the gradient as the fastest increase leads to gradient descent, an optimization technique to minimize a function. This technique is widely used in machine learning.
In coordinate-free terms, the gradient ∇f may be defined by:
df=∇f⋅d𝐫
where df is the total infinitesimal change in f for an infinitesimal displacement d𝐫, and is seen to be maximal when d𝐫 is in the direction of the gradient ∇f.
In a Cartesian coordinate system, the gradient is a vector of partial derivatives. For f:ℝn→ℝ, its gradient ∇f:ℝn→ℝn is defined at the point p=(x1,…,xn) as the vector
∇f(p)=[∂f∂x1(p)⋮∂f∂xn(p)].
(See § Cartesian coordinates for the conditions under which the above formula applies).
The gradient is dual to the total derivative df; see § Relationship with total derivative. It also admits multiple generalizations to more general functions on manifolds; see § Generalizations.

Motivation

Consider a room where the temperature is given by a scalar field, T, so at each point (x, y, z) the temperature is T(x, y, z), independent of time. At each point in the room, the gradient of T at that point will show the direction in which the temperature rises most quickly, moving away from (x, y, z). The magnitude of the gradient will determine how fast the temperature rises in that direction.
Consider a surface whose height above sea level at point (x, y) is H(x, y). The gradient of H at a point is a plane vector pointing in the direction of the steepest slope or grade at that point. The steepness of the slope at that point is given by the magnitude of the gradient vector.
The gradient can also be used to measure how a scalar field changes in other directions, rather than just the direction of greatest change, by taking a dot product. Suppose that the steepest slope on a hill is 40%. A road going directly uphill has slope 40%, but a road going around the hill at an angle will have a shallower slope. For example, if the road is at a 60° angle from the uphill direction (when both directions are projected onto the horizontal plane), then the slope along the road will be the dot product between the gradient vector and a unit vector along the road, as the dot product measures how much the unit vector along the road aligns with the steepest slope, which is 40% times the cosine of 60°, or 20%.
